Thanks again for a productive call this morning, Priya & Alex — good to meet the Ember team. Below is a short recap and concrete next steps so nothing slips.

High-level goals you called out:
- User-facing assistant (triage + long-form summarization) integrated into care workflows.
- Latency target: p95 under production-like load for short responses (<=128 tokens). We discussed 150ms as a target, but asked for confirmation.
- Throughput/concurrency: estimate ~200-300 concurrent active sessions during peak hours, bursty patterns.
- Streaming: required for narrative answers >256 tokens to reduce perceived latency and enable progressive render in the UI.
- Context window: customer wants to include ~6–8k tokens of patient context (notes + recent messages); output generative responses expected up to ~1k tokens in longest cases.

Operational constraints you mentioned:
- Sensitive data (PHI) — will need VPC/private deployment or strong guarantees on data handling and audit logs.
- Procurement: 6–8 week window, security questionnaire in flight.

Immediate next steps (proposed):
1) Technical deep-dive with Marcus (solutions) + engineering — to validate latency envelope and streaming approach (I propose Tues 18 Aug, 11am PT).
2) You to share a 48–72 hour sample of typical request/response payloads (anonymized) and expected concurrency cadence so we can run a small perf sim.
3) We'll prepare a short Map document with options: hosted with dedicated pool canary, or private VPC deployment for PHI — attached draft.

Thanks — I'll coordinate scheduling.

Kimberly / Laura — quick tech notes before the Tues sync so we have a starting hypothesis: 

1) Latency envelope (short responses)
- For short generations (<=128 output tokens) on a single GPU-backed dedicated pool, expect p95 in the 80–160ms range depending on model family and batching. p99 tails are typically 2–3x p95 unless we apply tail-mitigation (pre-warming, priority routing, isolated worker pools).

2) Concurrency & throughput
- 250 median concurrent sessions with spikes to 400 will benefit from: 1) horizontal worker pools (N small GPUs with 2–4 worker processes each) and 2) a request router that favors low-latency instances for small requests. Continuous batching helps cost but can add ~5–25ms; keep batch windows small (~5–10ms) for UX-sensitive paths.

3) Streaming behavior
- Chunked decode (streaming) yields much lower perceived latency for long outputs; doing incremental flushes at 64–128 token intervals reduces client wait time. Server-side cost is similar but network/serialization overhead rises.
- For outputs >512 tokens, p99 tail becomes important; streaming plus a separate high-throughput lane (bigger batch windows, quantized models) can reduce p99 by 30–40% versus a single mixed pool.

4) Context window & fallback
- 6–8k token context is fine on modern 8k/16k models; if customer wants to include full patient history (12k+), recommend either: a) on-the-fly summarization pipeline to reduce context, or b) dynamic KV-cache spilling with a summarization fallback for older segments. Both approaches trade slight QA with latency gains.

5) Model/quantization suggestions (private/on-prem)
- Strong candidates: Llama-3-8k-7B (q4f16) for high throughput with streaming; Llama-3-16k-13B (q4f16) for heavier context but higher latency. If strict p95 SLAs are required, prefer smaller lower-parameter variants with more workers.

6) Next validation steps
- Run a 48h perf sim using anonymized samples (preferably NGINX logs + request bodies) — we'll produce p50/p95/p99 under load and a streaming vs non-streaming comparison.
- We'll supply a short profiling CSV (profiling-run-summary-8k.csv) and a recommended canary config for dedicated pool sizing.

I can bring concrete numbers and a simple sizing matrix to Tues.

— Marcus Lin
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Our alignment:
- Contract-level target: we'll model for p95 <= 200ms for short responses and surface p99 estimates during the perf sim.
- Concurrency planning: we'll size for median 250 with headroom to 400 for bursts; proposed canary config will include an autoscale burst allowance.
- Streaming: we'll recommend chunked flushes at 64–128 tokens and a separate lane for long narratives to protect tail latency.
- Private/VPC: Marcus will include notes on KV cache isolation and what artifacts we can provide for security review.

What we need from Ember to run the perf sim:
1) 48–72h anonymized request/response samples + expected peak schedule (hourly cadence).
2) A short list of 5 representative long chat examples (synthesized/anonymized) to validate streaming and summarization fallback.

- Ember: share the anonymized samples and proc timeline (ETA: EOW Aug 21).
